prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. For large urban intersections and traffic roads of larger scale, adopt smaller curb radii and prudently set up... Set channelized facilities to shorten crossing distances at intersections; bicycle waiting areas may be provided in areas where conditions permit. For residential streets with heavy pedestrian flows, compact intersections or raised intersections may be adopted to reduce vehicle speeds. Public transit travel scenarios. Enrich the service functions of the stop area, strengthen integrated bus stop design, and coordinate the layout of shelters, trash bins, public toilets, and other facilities, while providing barrier-free ramps. Improve the convenience of bus transfers and use: bus stops should be located as close as possible to community entrances and metro entrances, with parking areas for non-motorized vehicles and shared bicycles; in areas where conditions permit, covered walkways may directly connect the stop with surrounding buildings. Rail transit travel scenarios. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:

 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2. (4) Transportation scenarios. Pedestrian crossing scenario. Give priority to ensuring safe and convenient pedestrian crossing. For large urban intersections and traffic roads of larger scale, adopt smaller curb radii and prudently set up... Set channelized facilities to shorten crossing distances at intersections; bicycle waiting areas may be provided in areas where conditions permit. For residential streets with heavy pedestrian flows, compact intersections or raised intersections may be adopted to reduce vehicle speeds. Public transit travel scenarios. Around urban bus stops, priority should be given to traffic transfer and the needs of special groups. Enrich the service functions of the stop area, strengthen integrated bus stop design, and coordinate the layout of shelters, trash bins, public toilets, and other facilities, while providing barrier-free ramps. Improve the convenience of bus transfers and use: bus stops should be located as close as possible to community entrances and metro entrances, with parking areas for non-motorized vehicles and shared bicycles; in areas where conditions permit, covered walkways may directly connect the stop with surrounding buildings. Rail transit travel scenarios. At rail transit entrances and exits, priority should be given to traffic gathering and dispersal functions, while coordinating the needs of special groups, and providing plaza space for gathering and dispersal, a clear wayfinding signage system, small resting spaces, and a complete barrier-free facility system. Concentrated parking areas for non-motorized vehicles, public bicycles, and shared bicycles shall be set up, and emergency evacuation routes shall be clearly marked. In areas where conditions permit, corner plazas and pocket parks may be added; it is encouraged to integrate breakfast stalls, convenience stores, and other convenience service facilities with station entrances and exits, and to provide covered walkways between rail transit stations and surrounding public buildings. (5) Work scenarios. — 8 — Express delivery and meal delivery scenarios. Based on the needs of waiting and delivery services for express delivery and meal delivery, dedicated temporary parking spaces shall be delineated at the entrances and exits of large commercial facilities. Shopping malls and stores are encouraged to set up rest areas for couriers and meal delivery riders, as well as shared toilets, to create a harmonious street atmosphere. In areas where conditions permit, existing street facilities such as newsstands may be integrated to arrange service stations in a coordinated manner, providing one-stop solutions for various needs during work, such as water replenishment and charging, while also offering shelter from wind and rain.
